steps.label: Ch. 4 roadmap
steps.speakerNotes: Level: undergraduate (year 3). Made from the lecture lec05-kp00 with view-from-text-v3: pages were planned first and each page is mainly one native infographic (designed in HTML and converted to native nodes), with the terms defined on the same page. 8 pages; this unit is an overview that only reviews and defines terms in plain language, adding no new content.

steps.label: The question
steps.speakerNotes: This is the first page of the chapter 4 roadmap. Three prerequisites: linear classifiers, scores, and coordinates with small tables. A linear classifier separates two classes with one line, calling A when the score is positive and B otherwise. The starting point of the chapter is exclusive OR, XOR: B when the two inputs are equal and A when they differ, so (0,0) and (1,1) are B and (0,1) and (1,0) are A. The two A points lie on one diagonal and the two B points on the other, and no straight line can put the two A points on one side and the two B points on the other. The chapter asks one question: how does a network separate labels that one line cannot? Next, the next page covers the roadmap.

steps.label: Roadmap
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on the chapter's question. This page is the roadmap of the whole chapter. The chapter has five KPs, one after another, and each starts from the question the previous one left over. KP01, one line is not enough, asks whether any line separates XOR and leaves the need to change the combination of boundaries. KP02, encode first and then classify, leaves the question whether the output layer is still enough with more lines. KP03, codes and limits, leaves the point that a labeling that cannot be cut needs another layer. KP04, detecting code by code, leaves the fact that it only proves sufficiency and the question of how a network grows from points. KP05, growing a network from points, leaves the point that all right holds only for this batch, so fix the architecture first and then learn the weights. Next, the next page covers the five words.

steps.label: Five words
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on the roadmap. This page gives five words in plain language first; later KPs unfold each one. Bit: a number that is only 0 or 1; a line asks whether the point is on the positive side and the answer is recorded as one bit. Hidden layer: the row of computing units between the inputs and the final output, each asking one small question. Code: all bits of a point written together, for example (1, 0), like a position label attached to the point. Unrealized code: a code that can be written down but that no input point gets. Detector: a unit that answers yes only when the input code equals one particular target code. Next, the next page covers KP01 and KP02.

steps.label: KP01 and KP02
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on the five words. This page gives the question, answer and what is left over for KP01 and KP02. KP01 asks whether any line separates XOR; the answer is that the two A scores must add up to a positive number and the two B scores to at most 0, yet it is the same expression, a contradiction; left over: what must change is the combination of boundaries, for example two lines that make a strip. KP02 asks how to build the two judgments as a network; the answer is that two lines give one bit each, the four points get only three codes, and one output line separates A from B; left over: with more lines, is the output layer still enough? Next, the next page covers KP03 and KP04.

steps.label: KP03 and KP04
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on KP01 and KP02. This page gives the question, answer and what is left over for KP03 and KP04. KP03 asks whether one cutting plane can separate every labeling once there are more lines; the answer is that some can and some cannot, for example when A and B alternate along the diagonal of the base; left over: a labeling that cannot be cut needs another layer. KP04 asks how to add another layer on top of the codes; the answer is that the detector score equals 0.5 minus the number of mismatched bits and the output layer merges with OR; left over: it only proves sufficiency, so how does a network grow from points? Next, the next page covers KP05 and the core figures.

steps.label: KP05, figures
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on KP03 and KP04. This page first covers KP05. Question: with only labeled points, how does a network grow; answer: a primary node splits once, auxiliary nodes handle the mixed groups and added bits purify them; left over: all right holds only for this batch of points, so fix the architecture first and then learn the weights. The five core figures below each match one KP: KP01 two parallel lines make a strip with A inside; KP02 builds it as a two-layer network; KP03 shows the limit of one cutting plane; KP04 adds another layer on the codes; KP05 shows how a network grows when none is given. Next, the next page covers the whole network.

steps.label: Whole network
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on KP05 and the core figures. This page reviews the four stages of the whole network: the input is the coordinates of the point; the hidden code is one bit per line joined into a code; the detectors answer yes only when the code equals the target code; the output merges the detectors with OR and calls A or B. Each stage takes only the result of the previous stage. Common myth: having built a network that suffices means the weights are learned or that the network is smallest. In fact a construction only proves sufficiency. Next, the next page covers the four reminders.

steps.label: Reminders
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on the whole network. This page gives the four reminders. First, on fixed codes one cutting plane has a limit. Second, contradictory labels cannot all be right. Third, all right means all right on this batch of points. Fourth, a construction proves sufficiency, not that the weights are learned or the network is smallest. Next chapter: fix the network architecture first and then learn the weights with a cost function, that is, backpropagation, starting at KP06. That ends this unit; next, move on to the next unit.
